subject: physics

items.q: A flat rectangular loop of wire measures 4.0 cm by 5.0 cm. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.30 T, with the plane of the loop at an angle of 30° to the field lines. What is the magnetic flux through the loop?
items.why:
The angle that is easiest to see in a diagram is between the field lines and the coil itself, and other equations (such as W = Fs cos θ) use the angle between the two drawn lines. The normal to a surface is an abstract line that is not usually drawn. Draw the normal to the coil and measure θ from it. A check: when the field passes straight through the coil face, the flux must be greatest, so cos θ must be 1 and θ = 0°; this is when the plane is perpendicular to the field. If the plane makes an angle α with the field, θ = 90° − α.

Working: A = 0.040 m × 0.050 m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². The angle between the field and the plane is 30°, so the angle between the field and the normal is θ = 60°. Φ = BA cos θ = (0.30 T)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(cos 60°) = (0.30)(2.0 × 10⁻³)(0.50) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb.
items.specStatementText: magnetic flux Φ as given by Φ = BA cos θ
items.working: A = 0.040 m × 0.050 m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². The angle between the field and the plane is 30°, so the angle between the field and the normal is θ = 60°. Φ = BA cos θ = (0.30 T)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(cos 60°) = (0.30)(2.0 × 10⁻³)(0.50) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb.

items.q: A flat loop of wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field. In which situation is the magnetic flux through the loop zero?
items.correct: Its plane is parallel to the field lines, so no field lines pass through the loop.
items.misconception: It is held at rest in the field, so the field through it is not changing.
items.why: The word "flux" suggests a flow, and flux is introduced alongside induction, where only CHANGES of flux matter. Students therefore merge flux with its rate of change and link both to motion. Separate the two quantities: Φ is how much field passes through the coil at an instant; ΔΦ/Δt is how quickly that changes. A coil at rest in a steady field has a constant Φ and zero ΔΦ/Δt, so it has flux but no induced emf.
items.specStatementText: magnetic flux Φ as given by Φ = BA cos θ
items.random_wrong: Its plane is perpendicular to the field lines, so θ in Φ = BA cos θ is 90°.

items.q: According to Faraday's law of induction, the magnitude of the emf induced in a coil with a fixed number of turns is proportional to which quantity?
items.correct: The rate at which the magnetic flux through the coil changes
items.misconception: The magnetic flux passing through the coil at that instant
items.why: The words flux, flux change and rate of change of flux appear together and are easily merged. Everyday reasoning also says that "more magnetism" should give "more electricity", and for an approaching magnet the flux and the emf both increase together, which seems to confirm it. Use Faraday's law literally: ε depends on ΔΦ/Δt, the gradient of a flux–time graph, not on its value. A coil at rest near a strong magnet has large flux and zero emf; a rotating coil has its largest emf when its flux passes through zero.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.random_wrong: The change in magnetic flux, whatever time it takes

items.q: A flat rectangular coil of 100 turns measures 4.0 cm by 5.0 cm. It starts with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.40 T and is then rotated through 60° in 0.050 s, about an axis perpendicular to the field. What is the magnitude of the average emf induced during the rotation?
items.why:
Students remember "change in flux" from Faraday's law and drop the "per unit time", especially when ΔΦ is the part of the calculation that takes the most work. Answers are then left in webers but labelled volts. ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt: after finding ΔΦ, always divide by the time taken. A useful check is units: Wb divided by s gives V, whereas NΔΦ alone is in Wb.

Working: A = 0.040 m × 0.050 m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². Initially the plane is perpendicular to the field, so θ = 0° and Φ₁ = BA = (0.40 T)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m²) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. After rotating 60°, θ = 60° and Φ₂ = BA cos 60° = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. ΔΦ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. Average ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × (4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb)/(0.050 s) = 0.80 V.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.working: A = 0.040 m × 0.050 m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². Initially the plane is perpendicular to the field, so θ = 0° and Φ₁ = BA = (0.40 T)(2.0 × 10⁻³ m²) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. After rotating 60°, θ = 60° and Φ₂ = BA cos 60° = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. ΔΦ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. Average ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × (4.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb)/(0.050 s) = 0.80 V.

items.q: A small flat coil is held at rest inside a long solenoid, with its plane perpendicular to the solenoid's axis. The magnetic field in the solenoid is proportional to the current in it. The current rises steadily from 0 to 2.0 A between t = 0 and t = 4.0 s, stays at 2.0 A until t = 8.0 s, and then falls steadily to zero by t = 10.0 s. Which describes the emf induced in the small coil?
items.correct: Constant from 0 to 4 s, zero from 4 to 8 s, then reversed and larger in size from 8 to 10 s
items.misconception: Zero throughout, because the small coil is at rest and nothing moves relative to it
items.why:
Induction is usually first demonstrated by moving a magnet in and out of a coil and described as "cutting field lines", so students tie induction to motion rather than to a change of flux. Faraday's law needs only a changing flux, ΔΦ/Δt ≠ 0. Flux can change because B changes (a time-varying field), because A or θ changes (a rotating coil), or because the conductor moves (relative motion). The first involves no motion at all.

Working: The flux through the small coil is proportional to the solenoid current, so the emf is proportional to the rate of change of current. 0 to 4.0 s: ΔI/Δt = (2.0 A)/(4.0 s) = +0.50 A s⁻¹, constant, so the emf is constant. 4.0 s to 8.0 s: ΔI/Δt = 0, so the emf is zero. 8.0 s to 10.0 s: ΔI/Δt = (−2.0 A)/(2.0 s) = −1.0 A s⁻¹, so the emf is reversed and twice the size it was from 0 to 4.0 s.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.random_wrong: Constant from 0 to 4 s, zero from 4 to 8 s, then reversed but the same size from 8 to 10 s
items.working: The flux through the small coil is proportional to the solenoid current, so the emf is proportional to the rate of change of current. 0 to 4.0 s: ΔI/Δt = (2.0 A)/(4.0 s) = +0.50 A s⁻¹, constant, so the emf is constant. 4.0 s to 8.0 s: ΔI/Δt = 0, so the emf is zero. 8.0 s to 10.0 s: ΔI/Δt = (−2.0 A)/(2.0 s) = −1.0 A s⁻¹, so the emf is reversed and twice the size it was from 0 to 4.0 s.

items.q: A flat square coil connected to a data logger moves at constant velocity, with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. It starts outside the field, passes into it, crosses it and leaves on the far side. The field region is wider than the coil. Which describes the induced emf?
items.correct: Constant while entering, zero while wholly inside, then reversed while leaving
items.misconception: Constant while entering, zero while wholly inside, then in the same direction while leaving
items.why: Lenz's law is usually taught with a magnet being pushed INTO a coil, where the coil repels it, and "opposes" is remembered as "opposes the field" or "pushes back" rather than "opposes the change". Ask what is changing. If the flux through the coil is increasing, the induced field opposes it (points against the external field); if the flux is decreasing, the induced field tries to maintain it (points along the external field). A coil therefore repels an approaching magnet but attracts a receding one: it always opposes the relative motion.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.random_wrong: Rising steadily while entering, largest while wholly inside, then falling to zero while leaving

items.q: A metal rod 0.40 m long rests across two parallel horizontal rails 0.40 m apart, which are joined at one end by a resistor. A uniform vertical magnetic field of strength 150 mT acts over the whole arrangement. The rod moves along the rails at constant velocity, away from the resistor, so that it travels 1.0 m in the next 0.50 s. At the instant considered it is 0.15 m from the resistor. What is the emf induced in the rod?
items.why:
Laboratory magnetic fields are usually quoted in mT, and the prefix is easy to overlook when the number looks like an ordinary value. The resulting emfs, hundreds of volts from a rod on rails, are not checked for plausibility. Convert every quantity to base SI units first: 1 mT = 10⁻³ T. Then check the answer: a rod moving at a few m s⁻¹ in a laboratory field gives an emf of a fraction of a volt, never hundreds of volts.

Working: v = 1.0 m / 0.50 s = 2.0 m s⁻¹. B = 150 mT = 0.150 T. The rod (L = 0.40 m), its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular, so ε = BvL = (0.150 T)(2.0 m s⁻¹)(0.40 m) = 0.12 V.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces an emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicularly to it as given by ε = BvL
items.working: v = 1.0 m / 0.50 s = 2.0 m s⁻¹. B = 150 mT = 0.150 T. The rod (L = 0.40 m), its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular, so ε = BvL = (0.150 T)(2.0 m s⁻¹)(0.40 m) = 0.12 V.

items.q: A flat square coil of 100 turns and side 5.0 cm moves at a constant 0.60 m s⁻¹ into a region of uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 T. The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field and its leading side is parallel to the edge of the field region. What is the emf induced in the coil while it is entering the field?
items.why:
For a rotating coil the two long sides DO both contribute and their emfs add, giving 2NBvL. Students carry this result over to a coil moving in a straight line without checking which sides are actually in the field. Check which sides are inside the field and how they move. Entering: only the leading side cuts field lines, ε = NBvL. Wholly inside: both sides have equal emfs that oppose each other around the loop, total zero. Leaving: only the trailing side cuts field lines, ε = NBvL in the opposite direction.

Working: While entering, only the leading side (L = 0.050 m) cuts field lines (the trailing side is still outside the field; the sides parallel to the motion move along their own length). ε = NBvL = 100 × (0.20 T)(0.60 m s⁻¹)(0.050 m) = 0.60 V. Check with Faraday's law: time to enter Δt = 0.050 m / 0.60 m s⁻¹ = 0.0833 s; ΔΦ per turn = BL² = 0.20 × 0.0025 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb; ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.0833 = 0.60 V.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces an emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicularly to it as given by ε = BvL
items.working: While entering, only the leading side (L = 0.050 m) cuts field lines (the trailing side is still outside the field; the sides parallel to the motion move along their own length). ε = NBvL = 100 × (0.20 T)(0.60 m s⁻¹)(0.050 m) = 0.60 V. Check with Faraday's law: time to enter Δt = 0.050 m / 0.60 m s⁻¹ = 0.0833 s; ΔΦ per turn = BL² = 0.20 × 0.0025 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ Wb; ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.0833 = 0.60 V.

items.q: A straight copper rod is held horizontal and at right angles to a uniform horizontal magnetic field. The ends of the rod are not connected to anything. In which case is an emf induced between the ends of the rod?
items.correct: The rod moves vertically upwards at a steady speed while staying horizontal.
items.misconception: The rod moves horizontally in the same direction as the field lines.
items.why: Demonstrations show that moving a wire near a magnet produces a meter reading, and the conclusion "motion in a field gives emf" is remembered without the condition that the motion must be across the field or change the flux. Ask whether the flux changes: a straight conductor must sweep across field lines (ε = BvL with v perpendicular to B); a closed coil must have the flux through it change. Motion along the field lines, or of a coil wholly inside a uniform field, changes nothing and induces no emf.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces an emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicularly to it as given by ε = BvL
items.random_wrong: The rod slides horizontally along the direction of its own length.

items.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed at a steady speed into a coil that is connected to a resistor, and the resistor warms up. Where does the energy transferred to the resistor come from?
items.correct: Work done by the person pushing the magnet against the opposing force from the coil
items.misconception: The magnet's store of magnetism, which is gradually used up by the induced current it produces
items.why: Magnets seem to be the "source" in induction experiments, and students are used to batteries running down as they supply energy. The idea that a magnet is a store of energy that is gradually used up follows naturally. A permanent magnet is not an energy store that is emptied by induction; it can be used indefinitely. The induced current produces a force that opposes the motion, so whatever moves the magnet does work against that force, and that work becomes electrical energy and then internal energy of the circuit.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: The coil's attraction of the magnet, which pulls it in and does work on it

items.q: A strong bar magnet is released from rest and falls vertically down the centre of a long vertical copper tube. How does its fall compare with a fall from rest through the same height in air outside the tube?
items.correct: It falls more slowly, because currents induced in the tube exert forces that oppose its motion.
items.misconception: It falls in the same way, because copper is not magnetic and so exerts no force on it.
items.why: Students learn early that only iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted by magnets, and generalise this to "magnets do not affect other metals". The forces from induced currents act only during motion, so everyday experience with stationary magnets supports the belief. Distinguish magnetic attraction of ferromagnetic materials from electromagnetic induction. Any conductor in a changing flux has an emf induced in it; in a solid conductor this drives circulating currents, which by Lenz's law oppose the relative motion. A magnet dropped down a copper tube falls slowly for this reason.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: It falls faster, because the currents induced in the tube pull it downwards.

items.q: A bar magnet hangs vertically from a spring and oscillates up and down just above a flat coil. When the ends of the coil are unconnected, the oscillations die away very slowly. When the ends are joined through a resistor, the oscillations die away much faster. Which explains the difference?
items.correct: With the ends joined a current flows, and its force opposes the motion, transferring energy to the resistor.
items.misconception: An emf is induced in the coil only once its ends are joined, so only then can the coil affect the magnet at all.
items.why: Induced emf is usually detected with a meter or lamp in a complete circuit, and students do not separate emf (energy per unit charge) from current (flow of charge). Everyday language uses "electricity" for both. Separate cause and effect: a changing flux induces an emf; the emf drives a current only if there is a complete circuit. An open coil still has an emf across its ends, which a voltmeter or oscilloscope can measure.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: With the ends joined, the coil repels the magnet at every point of its motion, reducing its amplitude.

items.q: The current in a long coil is decreasing steadily. There is no magnet or other circuit nearby. Which statement about any emf induced in the coil is correct?
items.correct: An emf is induced in the same direction as the current, tending to keep the current flowing.
items.misconception: An emf is induced opposite in direction to the current, making the current fall faster.
items.why: Self-induced emf is often called a "back emf", and its best-known effect, slowing the rise of current when a circuit is switched on, is an example where it opposes the current. Students generalise this to every case. Apply Lenz's law to the change: if the current falls, the flux falls, and the induced emf tries to keep the flux, so it drives charge in the SAME direction as the current. This is why breaking a circuit containing a large coil can produce a spark across the switch.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: No emf is induced, because a coil's own changing field cannot induce an emf in it.

items.q: A flat rectangular coil rotates at a constant frequency about an axis that lies in its own plane and is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. How does the magnitude of the induced emf depend on the position of the coil?
items.correct: It is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where the flux is zero.
items.misconception: It is the same at every position, because the coil turns at a steady rate in a uniform field.
items.why: Constant motion suggests a constant effect, and students picture the coil sides moving at constant speed without considering that the direction of that motion relative to the field changes throughout each revolution. The speed of each side is constant, but the component of its velocity perpendicular to the field is v sin θ, which varies from zero to v and back. Equivalently, Φ = BA cos θ changes fastest where the cosine graph is steepest, at θ = 90°.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces a sinusoidal varying emf in a coil rotating within it
items.random_wrong: It is greatest when the coil's plane is perpendicular to the field, where the flux through it is greatest.

items.q: A rectangular coil of 40 turns measures 6.0 cm by 4.0 cm. It rotates at a constant 25 revolutions per second about an axis through its centre, parallel to its 6.0 cm sides and perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.10 T. What is the peak emf induced in the coil?
items.why:
Frequency f and angular frequency ω = 2πf are easily confused, and v = ωr is remembered with f substituted for ω. The missing 2π is not noticed because the result still has units of m s⁻¹. In one revolution a side moves 2πr, and there are f revolutions per second, so v = 2πfr. Substitute ω = 2πf, not f, into v = ωr.

Working: r = 4.0 cm / 2 = 0.020 m; v = 2πfr = 2π × 25 s⁻¹ × 0.020 m = 3.14 m s⁻¹. At the peak the two 6.0 cm sides move perpendicular to the field; each has ε = BvL = (0.10 T)(3.14 m s⁻¹)(0.060 m) = 0.0188 V, and the two add around each turn. Peak ε = 2NBvL = 2 × 40 × 0.0188 V = 1.5 V. (The 4.0 cm sides have no emf along them.)
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces a sinusoidal varying emf in a coil rotating within it
items.working: r = 4.0 cm / 2 = 0.020 m; v = 2πfr = 2π × 25 s⁻¹ × 0.020 m = 3.14 m s⁻¹. At the peak the two 6.0 cm sides move perpendicular to the field; each has ε = BvL = (0.10 T)(3.14 m s⁻¹)(0.060 m) = 0.0188 V, and the two add around each turn. Peak ε = 2NBvL = 2 × 40 × 0.0188 V = 1.5 V. (The 4.0 cm sides have no emf along them.)

items.q: A coil rotating at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field produces an alternating emf with a time period of 20 ms. The rotation rate is then changed to 1800 revolutions per minute. What is the new time period of the emf?
items.why:
Frequency and time period are introduced together and both describe "how the cycle goes", so students scale them the same way. Proportional reasoning is applied without checking whether the relationship is direct or inverse. Always go through T = 1/f. Doubling f halves T; reducing f from 50 Hz to 30 Hz increases T from 20 ms to 33 ms.

Working: f = 1800 rev min⁻¹ / 60 s min⁻¹ = 30 Hz. The emf completes one cycle per revolution, so T = 1/f = 1/(30 Hz) = 0.0333 s = 3.3 × 10⁻² s.
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.working: f = 1800 rev min⁻¹ / 60 s min⁻¹ = 30 Hz. The emf completes one cycle per revolution, so T = 1/f = 1/(30 Hz) = 0.0333 s = 3.3 × 10⁻² s.

items.q: A rectangular coil rotates at a constant frequency in a uniform magnetic field. A graph of the induced emf against time is a sine curve that is zero at t = 0, 10 ms, 20 ms, 30 ms and 40 ms, with maxima of +4.0 V at 5 ms and 25 ms and minima of −4.0 V at 15 ms and 35 ms. The coil is then made to rotate at 40 revolutions per second in the same field. What is the new peak emf?
items.why:
On a sinusoidal graph the zeros are the most obvious marks, and a "hump" between two zeros looks like one complete wave. Students then read half a cycle as a full cycle. A cycle contains a positive half and a negative half. Measure from one positive peak to the next, or from one upward zero crossing to the next. If zeros are 10 ms apart, the period is 20 ms.

Working: Time between successive maxima (5 ms and 25 ms) = 20 ms, so T = 0.020 s and f₁ = 1/T = 50 Hz. Peak emf ∝ f, so ε₂ = 4.0 V × (40 Hz / 50 Hz) = 3.2 V.
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.working: Time between successive maxima (5 ms and 25 ms) = 20 ms, so T = 0.020 s and f₁ = 1/T = 50 Hz. Peak emf ∝ f, so ε₂ = 4.0 V × (40 Hz / 50 Hz) = 3.2 V.

items.q: The graph shows how the magnetic flux Φ through each turn of a coil of 200 turns varies with time t. The coil is held at rest. What is the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil between t = 0.50 s and t = 0.70 s?
items.why:
Φ is calculated for one turn, and students then substitute it into ε = ΔΦ/Δt from memory without the N. Treating the coil as "one wire" makes the omission seem reasonable. Every turn encloses the same changing flux, so every turn has the same emf, and series emfs add. Multiply the single-turn emf by N; a coil of 100 turns has 100 times the emf of a single loop.

Working: Between t = 0.50 s and t = 0.70 s the flux per turn falls in a straight line from 0.40 mWb to 0, so ΔΦ/Δt = (0 − 0.40 × 10⁻³ Wb)/(0.20 s) = −2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb s⁻¹ (the gradient of that segment of the graph). Faraday's law: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt = −200 × (−2.0 × 10⁻³) = +0.40 V. Magnitude 0.40 V (2 s.f.).
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.working: Between t = 0.50 s and t = 0.70 s the flux per turn falls in a straight line from 0.40 mWb to 0, so ΔΦ/Δt = (0 − 0.40 × 10⁻³ Wb)/(0.20 s) = −2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb s⁻¹ (the gradient of that segment of the graph). Faraday's law: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt = −200 × (−2.0 × 10⁻³) = +0.40 V. Magnitude 0.40 V (2 s.f.).

items.q: A flat square coil moves at constant velocity, with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, through a region of field that is wider than the coil. It starts outside the region, passes right through it and leaves on the far side. The graph shows the emf induced in the coil against time. Which conclusion follows from the graph?
items.correct: The field region is three times as wide as the coil.
items.misconception: The field region is exactly twice as wide as the coil.
items.why: Students picture the coil as a point moving into and out of the field. They forget that the flux is constant only once the trailing edge has entered and only until the leading edge starts to leave, so the entering and leaving phases (each lasting L/v) are part of the time the coil spends in the region. The emf is zero only while the flux is constant — from the instant the trailing edge enters until the leading edge reaches the far boundary. The leading edge travels W − L during that time, so zero-emf time = (W − L)/v, while each pulse of emf lasts L/v. The ratio of the two intervals gives (W − L)/L, not W/L.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.random_wrong: The flux through the coil is zero from t = 0.20 s to t = 0.60 s.

items.q: The diagram shows a metal rod PQ resting across two horizontal rails that are joined at their left-hand end by a resistor R. A uniform magnetic field acts into the page over the whole arrangement. The rod is pulled to the right at a constant speed v. Which statement about the induced current is correct?
items.correct: It flows in the rod from Q to P, so that end P is at the higher potential.
items.misconception: It flows in the rod from P to Q, driving the rod along the rails faster.
items.why: Students know that a current-carrying coil acts as a magnet and that magnets attract, and the direction rule is easily remembered the wrong way round. Without linking Lenz's law to energy, either direction seems equally plausible. Test the direction with energy: the induced current transfers energy to a resistor, so something must do work against a resisting force. If the coil attracted an approaching magnet, both the magnet's kinetic energy and the current would grow from nothing. The coil must therefore oppose the motion.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: It is zero, because the uniform field through the circuit is steady.

items.q: The diagram shows a bar magnet being moved towards a flat, closed circular loop of copper wire that lies horizontally below it. Which statement about the induced current, as seen by an observer looking down on the loop from above, is correct?
items.correct: Anticlockwise, and the person moving the magnet does work against the loop.
items.misconception: Clockwise, so that the loop pulls the magnet in and makes its approach faster.
items.why: Students know that a current-carrying coil acts as a magnet and that magnets attract, and the direction rule is easily remembered the wrong way round. Without linking Lenz's law to energy, either direction seems equally plausible. Test the direction with energy: the induced current transfers energy to a resistor, so something must do work against a resisting force. If the coil attracted an approaching magnet, both the magnet's kinetic energy and the current would grow from nothing. The coil must therefore oppose the motion.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.random_wrong: There is no current at all, because the loop is not made of a magnetic material.

items.q: A rectangular coil rotates at a constant frequency about an axis in its own plane, perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The graph shows the emf induced in the coil against time; P and Q are two instants marked on it. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: At Q the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field.
items.misconception: The flux through the coil at P is the same as the flux at Q.
items.why: B is often called "magnetic flux density" and field-line diagrams are described as showing "lines of flux", so the two words are used interchangeably. Students then think only B matters and ignore area and orientation. Φ = BA cos θ has three factors. In a uniform, steady field B is fixed, but rotating a coil changes θ and so changes Φ; turning the plane of the coil parallel to the field makes Φ zero even though the field is still there.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces a sinusoidal varying emf in a coil rotating within it
items.random_wrong: At Q the plane of the coil is parallel to the field.

figure.alt: Graph of induced emf ε against time t (the vertical axis is marked 0 at the time axis; no other numbers are given). The curve is a sine wave starting at zero when t = 0, rising to a positive peak, falling through zero to an equal negative trough, and returning to zero, repeated for two full cycles. Point P is marked at the first positive peak. Point Q is marked at the first zero after P, where the curve crosses the time axis on its way down from P to the trough.

items.q: The graph shows the emf induced in a coil that rotates at a constant frequency in a uniform magnetic field. The frequency of rotation is then doubled, with nothing else changed. What is the time period of the new emf?
items.correct: 20 ms
items.misconception: 40 ms
items.why:
In sketches of the emf–time graph at a new rotation frequency, students often change the height of the peaks but keep the original period. Experience of the mains supply, whose frequency is always the same, can reinforce the idea that an alternating emf has a fixed period. Follow the coil: the emf repeats every time the coil returns to the same position, that is, once per revolution. So T(emf) = 1/f(rotation), and any change in the rotation frequency changes the period of the emf.

Working: From the graph, one complete cycle (zero → peak → zero → trough → zero) takes 40 ms: the emf is zero at 0, 20 and 40 ms, but 0 to 20 ms is only half a cycle. So T = 40 ms and f = 1/T = 25 Hz. The emf goes through one cycle per revolution, so doubling the frequency of rotation to 50 Hz halves the time period: T_new = 1/50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms. (The peak emf also doubles, to 6.0 V, but that is not asked.)
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.random_wrong: 80 ms
items.working: From the graph, one complete cycle (zero → peak → zero → trough → zero) takes 40 ms: the emf is zero at 0, 20 and 40 ms, but 0 to 20 ms is only half a cycle. So T = 40 ms and f = 1/T = 25 Hz. The emf goes through one cycle per revolution, so doubling the frequency of rotation to 50 Hz halves the time period: T_new = 1/50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms. (The peak emf also doubles, to 6.0 V, but that is not asked.)

items.q: Is the flux through a coil in a uniform field always BA?
items.correct: No. Φ = BA only when the field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil. In general Φ = BA cos θ, which is smaller when the coil is tilted and zero when its plane is parallel to the field.
items.misconception: The flux through a coil is BA whatever the orientation of the coil, because B and A do not change when the coil is tilted.
items.why: Flux is often introduced with the special case of a field perpendicular to a surface, and Φ = BA is remembered as the definition. Students then treat the cos θ factor as an optional refinement rather than part of the definition. Flux counts how much field passes THROUGH the area. Tilting the coil reduces the area it presents across the field lines to A cos θ, so Φ = BA cos θ. Only when θ = 0° is Φ = BA.
items.specStatementText: magnetic flux Φ as given by Φ = BA cos θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is an area in cm² converted to m²?
items.correct: Divide by 10⁴, because 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10⁴ cm². So 20 cm² = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m².
items.misconception: An area in cm² is converted to m² by dividing by 100, the same factor as for lengths.
items.why: Students remember that 100 cm = 1 m and apply the same factor to squared units without squaring it. The error is common whenever areas are calculated from dimensions given in centimetres. Convert each length to metres BEFORE multiplying: 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm = 0.040 m × 0.050 m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². If you convert an area directly, divide by (100)² = 10⁴.
items.specStatementText: magnetic flux Φ as given by Φ = BA cos θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a straight conductor moving at right angles to a magnetic field always have an emf, whatever its orientation?
items.correct: No. ε = BvL needs v perpendicular to B AND to the length L of the conductor. A rod lying across a field and sliding along its own length does not sweep across any field lines, so no emf is induced between its ends.
items.misconception: A straight conductor has an emf BvL whenever it moves at right angles to the field, whatever the direction of its motion relative to its own length.
items.why: ε = BvL is learned with the single condition "moving at right angles to the field", and textbook diagrams always show the rod moving sideways, so the requirement that it move perpendicular to its own length is never noticed. Picture the area swept out per second: a rod sliding along its own length sweeps no area, so it cuts no flux. The magnetic force on its electrons, perpendicular to both v and B, then points across the rod rather than along it, and no emf builds up between the ends.
items.specStatementText: that a uniform magnetic field induces an emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicularly to it as given by ε = BvL
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a magnet attract every metal?
items.correct: No. Only ferromagnetic materials such as iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are attracted by a stationary magnet. Copper, aluminium and brass are not.
items.misconception: Magnets attract all metals, so a magnet near a copper or aluminium object will be pulled onto it.
items.why: The everyday objects a magnet picks up (paper clips, pins, fridge doors) are metal, so "magnets attract metal" is learned as a rule in primary school and is rarely corrected. Test the claim: a magnet does not stick to a copper pipe or an aluminium can. Copper affects a magnet only when there is relative motion, through induced currents that oppose the motion; it does not attract a magnet at rest.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a changing current in a coil induce an emf in that same coil?
items.correct: Yes. A changing current changes the flux through the coil's own turns, and by Faraday's law this induces an emf in the coil itself. This is self-induction.
items.misconception: An emf can be induced in a coil only by a separate magnet or a separate circuit; a coil's own magnetic field cannot induce an emf in itself.
items.why: Induction is introduced with two objects, a magnet and a coil or two coils, so students think of it as one object acting on another. The idea of a coil acting on itself is not met in these first examples. Faraday's law does not ask where the flux comes from. The turns of a coil sit in the field produced by their own current, so when that current changes, the flux through the turns changes and an emf is induced in them.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a conductor in a strong steady magnetic field have an emf induced in it?
items.correct: No. A steady field, however strong, induces no emf in a stationary conductor. An emf is induced only when the flux linked with the conductor changes.
items.misconception: A conductor placed in a magnetic field has an emf induced in it even when nothing moves or changes, and the stronger the field, the larger the emf.
items.why: Students know that magnets "make electricity" in generators and do not separate the presence of a field from a change of flux. The name "flux density" for B also encourages the belief that a strong field means strong induction. A coil left at rest next to the strongest magnet gives no reading on a meter; the reading appears only while the magnet or coil moves, or while the field changes. The emf depends on ΔΦ/Δt, not on B itself.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the peak emf of a generator depend on how fast its coil rotates?
items.correct: Yes. The peak emf is proportional to the frequency of rotation: at twice the frequency the flux changes by the same amount in half the time, so the peak emf doubles.
items.misconception: Rotating the coil faster only makes the emf alternate more often; the peak emf depends only on N, B and the area of the coil, so it is unchanged.
items.why: The flux through the coil swings between the same limits, ±BA, at any speed, so students think the "size" of the effect is fixed and only its timing changes. Graph sketches in exams often keep the same peak with more cycles. Faraday's law depends on the RATE of change of flux. At frequency 2f the flux goes from +BA to −BA in half the time, so ΔΦ/Δt, and the peak emf, doubles. Faster rotation gives both taller and closer-spaced peaks.
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a rotation rate in revolutions per minute be used directly as a frequency in Hz?
items.correct: No. Revolutions per minute must be divided by 60 to give revolutions per second (Hz). 1800 rev min⁻¹ = 30 Hz.
items.misconception: A rotation rate in revolutions per minute can be used directly as the frequency in hertz.
items.why: Motors and generators are often rated in rev min⁻¹ (rpm), and students substitute the number without noticing that the hertz means "per second". The resulting periods of fractions of a millisecond are not checked for plausibility. Convert to per second first: f = (rev min⁻¹)/60. Then T = 1/f. A check: a generator turning 1800 times a minute turns 30 times a second, so one turn takes about 0.03 s.
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the peak emf of a rotating coil proportional to the time period of its rotation?
items.correct: No. The peak emf is proportional to the frequency of rotation, f = 1/T, so it is inversely proportional to the time period: a longer period (slower rotation) gives a SMALLER peak emf.
items.misconception: The peak emf of a rotating coil is proportional to the time period of its rotation, so a longer period gives a larger peak emf.
items.why: Students reason that a slowly turning coil spends longer in each position and so has "more time" to induce an emf, merging the total change of flux in a cycle with its rate of change. On an emf–time graph the period is the quantity read directly, so proportional reasoning is applied to T rather than to f. Faraday's law depends on the RATE of change of flux. The flux swings between the same limits, ±BA, in every revolution, so a longer period means a slower change and a smaller emf. Convert the period to a frequency first (f = 1/T) and scale the peak emf with f.
items.specStatementText: the effect on induced emf caused by changing the frequency of rotation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is it harder to push a magnet into a coil when the coil is connected to a resistor than when its ends are unconnected?
items.correct: Yes. With the coil connected, the induced current makes the coil repel the approaching magnet, so extra force and extra work are needed; that work is the energy transferred to the resistor. With the ends unconnected there is an emf but no current, no opposing force and no energy transfer.
items.misconception: Induction creates electrical energy without any extra work: a magnet is no harder to push into a coil connected to a resistor than into an unconnected coil.
items.why: Induction is described as the changing flux "producing" electricity, which makes the flux change sound like the energy source. In classroom demonstrations with a small coil and a meter the opposing force is far too small to feel, so electrical energy seems to appear without any extra effort. Compare the two cases. Unconnected coil: emf but no current, so no force from the coil. Connected coil: the induced current makes the coil repel the magnet (Lenz's law), so the pusher does extra work, and energy conservation requires exactly this, because the resistor gains energy. The larger the current, the harder the magnet is to push.
items.specStatementText: that the direction of induced emf is determined by Lenz’s law and is a consequence of energy conservation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A flux–time graph has its vertical axis labelled Φ / mWb. Can the numbers read from it be put straight into ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt?
items.correct: No. The axis label means the numbers are in milliweber; each must be multiplied by 10⁻³ to give the flux in weber before the emf comes out in volts.
items.misconception: Values read from an axis labelled Φ / mWb can be substituted directly into ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt; the prefix in the axis label makes no difference to the emf.
items.why: Numbers on a graph are read as bare numbers. The '/ mWb' in an IB axis label is easily skipped, so the milli prefix is lost — the same slip as putting a field quoted in mT straight into ε = BvL. An IB axis label 'Φ / mWb' means the plotted number is Φ divided by 1 mWb, so Φ = (number) × 10⁻³ Wb. Convert before substituting, exactly as mT must be converted to T. A change of 0.40 mWb in 0.20 s is a rate of 2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb s⁻¹, not 2.0 Wb s⁻¹, and the emf of a 200-turn coil is 0.40 V, not 400 V.
items.specStatementText: that a time-changing magnetic flux induces an emf ε as given by Faraday’s law of induction ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
